findings.name: A thread waits for a signal that already came
findings.impact: A thread signalled while nobody was waiting, so the signal was thrown away; the thread that waits afterwards sleeps for good, and whoever waits for it hangs too.
findings.summary: work[1] signalled condition variable 0x00000054cea8c018 at 9663.90 ms when no thread was waiting on it, then joined mc-log. mc-log only began its wait 693.85 ms later and was still blocked 3643.04 ms on, until the end of the trace, with no further signal: the program is hung.
findings.qnx: pthread_cond_signal() wakes a thread that is already waiting; with no waiter the signal is lost. Wait in a loop that re-checks the condition while holding the mutex (the thread that sets the condition must also hold the mutex), and test the stop flag before every wait.

radar.name: mc-log
radar.summary: mc-log (prio 10) behaved unlike healthy QNX programs in 182 of its 225 time windows; the most unusual stretch lasted 3640 ms. It stands out in: time waiting on a condition variable (higher than healthy), longest single block (higher than healthy), time asleep (lower than healthy). The closest pattern TraceLens has seen is priority inversion while waiting on a condition variable, but only loosely (distance 9.83 against 0.847 typical for it): treat this as behaviour of its own.

remedies.title: Re-check 'do_run_logger_thread' under the lock before the wait: if ((watcher_count == 0) && do_run_logger_thread)
remedies.rationale: pthread_cond_signal() wakes only a thread that is already waiting. The stopper sets the flag and signals under the mutex, but the waiter tests only its own idle condition before it waits, so a stop that lands while the waiter is not yet waiting is lost and the waiter sleeps forever. Testing the flag under the same mutex, in the same condition that guards the wait, makes the two orderings equivalent: either the waiter sees the flag and skips the wait, or it is already waiting when the signal arrives.
